opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is something we looked at pretty directly in our work on the energy cost of AI inference. We compared task-specific models, the kind fine-tuned to do one thing, like sentiment analysis or extractive question answering, against these general-purpose, multitask generative models that are being used for the same tasks now. And the difference was really striking. For a simple classification task, using a big generative model can consume orders of magnitude more energy than a small dedicated model, sometimes something like twenty or thirty times more, and in some cases much more than that, depending on the task and the model size.

The way I think about the trade-off is that there's this assumption that because a model *can* do everything, we should use it for everything. And sure, there's a convenience factor. You deploy one model, you don't have to maintain a zoo of specialized ones, and maybe you get a bit more flexibility. But you pay for that flexibility every single time you run a query, and at the scale these systems are deployed, with millions or billions of queries, that really adds up. Inference isn't a one-time cost like training. It's ongoing.

So my position isn't that multitask models are bad. They're incredibly useful for open-ended stuff, for creative tasks, for things where you genuinely don't know what the user is going to ask. But if you know you need to classify emails as spam or not spam, you don't need a seventy-billion-parameter model to do that. A small fine-tuned model will often do as well or better, faster and cheaper, and with a fraction of the carbon footprint.

What I'd really like to see is people making that choice consciously. Right now there's very little transparency. Users and even developers often have no idea how much energy a given model uses, so they can't factor it in. That's part of why we've been pushing for things like energy ratings for models, so that efficiency becomes one of the criteria people weigh alongside accuracy, rather than an afterthought. It's kind of like choosing the right tool for the job. You don't need a sledgehammer to hang a picture frame.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something we looked at pretty carefully in the "Power Hungry Processing" paper, and honestly the result surprised even me a little bit in terms of the magnitude.

The way I think about it is: there's a real tension between flexibility and efficiency. Multitask models, these big general-purpose models that you can throw any task at, are incredibly convenient. You don't have to train or deploy a separate model for question answering, for summarization, for classification. One model does it all. But what we found is that this convenience comes at a pretty steep energy cost. When we compared, say, a BERT-style model fine-tuned specifically for sentiment classification against a large generative model doing the same task through prompting, the difference wasn't ten or twenty percent. It was orders of magnitude. Something like thirty times more energy for the generative, multipurpose approach on the same task.

And the reason is kind of intuitive once you think about it. A single-task classifier is essentially outputting one number, a label. A generative model has to produce text token by token, and it's carrying all of this capacity that it doesn't actually need for that one task. You're paying for generality you're not using.

So the question I keep coming back to is: do you actually need the generality? Because in a lot of real deployments, people don't. They have a well-defined task, it's going to run millions of times a day, and they're using a general-purpose model because it's the default now, not because the task requires it. And when you multiply that per-query overhead by the scale of deployment, it adds up fast. Inference is where the volume is.

That said, I don't want to be too absolutist about it. There are cases where multitask genuinely makes sense. If you have a long tail of tasks, or your use case is open-ended and you really can't predict what users will ask, then maintaining fifty specialized models has its own costs, including the training cost of all those models. And there's an argument that one shared model amortizes its training energy across many uses.

But what bothers me is that this trade-off is almost never made explicitly. Nobody's sitting down and saying, okay, for this task, here's the efficiency we'd get from a specialized model versus the flexibility we'd get from a general one, and here's the energy delta. It's just, grab the biggest model, it works, ship it. And part of why that happens is we don't have good measurement or disclosure. If every deployment came with an energy figure, I think people would make different choices. So for me the trade-off question is less about which is always better and more about getting people to actually ask the question at all.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is whether you need that flexibility. A multitask model can do lots of different things, which is useful, but if you’re using it to do the same classification task over and over, you may be paying an energy cost for capabilities you don’t actually need.

There’s also a distinction between training and inference. Training one model that can handle multiple tasks could save you from training several separate models. But every time you use it, you’re running that more general model. If you’re serving millions of requests, that repeated inference cost can become really important.

So I’d compare models on the task you actually want to accomplish, at the quality you need. How much energy does it take to get a useful result? The flexibility of a multitask model has value, but it shouldn’t automatically be the default for every problem.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to compare them for the task you actually need to do. A multitask model gives you flexibility—you can use the same model for lots of different things—but that flexibility can come with an energy cost. If you’re using it for something a smaller, single-task model can do well, you may be spending more energy without getting a meaningful benefit.

You also have to consider training and deployment together. Training one model that serves many purposes could make sense, but inference adds up every time someone uses it. So the question is: What performance do you need, how often will you run it, and do you actually need that general-purpose capability? There isn’t one model that’s the most efficient choice for every situation.
